Week four, Thursday. Siddharth's second draft came back covered in pencil notes. He groaned, then fixed every line. Mahima finished her copying by eleven and scrolled her phone until lunch. Nobody asked what she had done that morning, and she stopped expecting anyone to.

Week eight, the last Friday. Mrs Pillai asked Siddharth to walk the finance head through his report. Mahima, packing her bag, tried to name one thing she had learned and couldn't. On the bus home she typed a note to herself: 'Next place, ask for real work.'

I sat in the car afterwards feeling I had been wrong about my own daughter. Now I bite my tongue. Yesterday the shopkeeper asked her which pencil she wanted, and I counted to five in my head. 14 Nov, night

Big fight with myself today. Jahnavi's school sent a form for the drama club. I almost wrote 'not interested' without asking her, because Jahnavi is the quiet one, everybody knows that. Then I remembered her at Diwali, explaining to her cousins how rockets work, loud and bossy, twenty minutes nonstop. Quiet with strangers, maybe. Not quiet. So I asked her. She shrugged and said, 'Can I just watch first?' Old me would have said 'see, shy' and ticked no. New me said, 'Watch first, then decide.' She's going on Friday. I'm nervous for her, which is silly. Darshan

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: The store announcement said the shop would close in ten minutes, and Tanvir was still holding the grey wool coat. 'Eleven thousand,' he muttered, and hung it back. Ishita, who had come only to help him find something for his sister's engagement, watched him grab a checked shirt from the next rack. The tag said 2,800. 'After that coat, this is basically free,' Tanvir said, already walking to the counter. Ishita frowned. Last week in the market he had refused a 900-rupee shirt as 'too much'. The lights began switching off section by section. 'Tanvir, wait. It's still twenty-eight hundred,' she said. He stopped, the shirt against his chest, and read the tag again. 'Huh. Said like that, it isn't cheap at all.' The guard called last billing. He bought it anyway, but slowly.

qa.q: What price was on the checked shirt's tag?
qa.a: The tag said 2,800.

qa.a: Ishita felt puzzled and concerned, remembering that only last week he had refused a 900-rupee shirt as too much.

qa.a: Before, it felt 'basically free' next to the coat; once he heard the number by itself, it no longer seemed cheap, though he still bought it.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: The salesman in the Pune showroom knew his job. First he brought out a suede jacket, 14,500, and let Dhruv try it on in front of the long mirror. Dhruv whistled at the tag and handed it back. Then, almost carelessly, the salesman laid a linen shirt on the counter: 3,200. 'Arre, that's reasonable, yaar,' Dhruv said to Hemant. Hemant said nothing. He was watching the order in which things had come out. At Dhruv's flat an hour later, his mother turned the bag over. 'Thirty-two hundred? For one shirt?' Dhruv opened his mouth to say it was cheap and stopped. Standing in his own kitchen, next to the vegetable basket and the electricity bill, it didn't look cheap at all. Hemant caught his eye and shrugged. 'It only looked small next to the jacket.'

qa.a: Hemant was curious and a little uneasy, noticing that the shirt only seemed reasonable because the costly jacket came first.

qa.a: Hemant could have gently asked Dhruv whether 3,200 would feel reasonable if he had seen the shirt first, so he could decide on the shirt alone.

qa.q: How does Dhruv's mother see the shirt?
qa.a: She sees only a shirt for thirty-two hundred, with no jacket beside it, so to her it looks expensive.

grounding: A friend watches a shopper call a costly shirt reasonable because an expensive jacket was seen just before it.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: Harish sat on the step of his shop in Mandsaur with the offer letter from the seed company folded in his shirt pocket. Twenty-two thousand a month, field work, a motorbike allowance. His cousin Divyansh, visiting from Indore, had laughed at it over lunch. 'My friend in Bengaluru gets three times that.' Harish had felt small for an hour. Now, alone, he took out a notebook and asked himself different questions. What does the shop bring in a normal month? What did I earn two years ago? What do Amma's medicines and the house need? He wrote two columns. The offer beat the shop and would give him evenings with his daughter. He looked at the Bengaluru figure once more, then crossed it out; that man didn't live in Mandsaur. He signed the letter.

qa.q: What did the seed company offer Harish?
qa.a: Twenty-two thousand a month, field work and a motorbike allowance.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after Divyansh's comment at lunch?
qa.a: Harish felt small and deflated for an hour, because the offer had been set against a big-city salary.

qa.q: What about Harish's approach could someone else use for a big choice?
qa.a: Compare the option with your own past, your real needs and the other options in front of you, rather than with someone else's life far away.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh see the offer differently from Harish?
qa.a: Divyansh measures it against a friend's city salary, while Harish measures it against the shop, his own past and his family's needs in Mandsaur.

grounding: An adult judges a job offer against his own past and needs rather than the nearest flashy example.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: Oskar was halfway through a friend's holiday photos when he caught himself sighing at his own Berlin flat: the one radiator, the crooked shelf, the view of the tram depot. Beach in Portugal. Rooftop dinner. New car. His thumb kept moving. He put the phone face down on the table. Elif, his flatmate, looked up from her laptop. 'You've got the face again.' 'Yeah.' He tried something his old football coach used to say: compare yourself with who you were. Two years ago he had been sleeping on his brother's sofa in Hamburg, with no contract. Now he had a job he liked and a room with a door. 'Honestly,' he said, 'this flat is fine. It's not a beach. It isn't meant to be.' Elif grinned and pushed the biscuit tin towards him.

qa.a: Putting the phone face down and comparing his life with his own past, not with friends' best moments.

qa.q: How does Elif see Oskar's change of mood?
qa.a: Elif spots 'the face again' and is glad to see him settle; pushing the biscuit tin over shows warmth and relief.

grounding: An adult stops measuring his life against friends' holiday highlights and compares it with his own past instead.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: At the nurses' station of the district hospital, Rajni read the transfer notice twice. Day shifts, children's ward, no more night duty. Jaya, eating upma beside her, peered over. 'Paeds? Priya got ICU in Chennai. That's a real career.' Rajni felt the old pinch. Priya's posts were all certificates and rooftop photos. Then she stopped and picked up a pen. Forget Priya, she thought. What do I actually want this year? Sleep. Time for my evening course. Less lifting while my back heals. Better than last year's nights? Yes, by a mile. She wrote 'YES' in the corner of the notice. Jaya raised an eyebrow. 'Just like that?' 'Not just like that,' Rajni said. 'I measured it against me, not against Priya.'

qa.a: Day shifts, with no more night duty.

qa.a: It was a sting of envy and self-doubt, from measuring her own move against Priya's ICU job and rooftop photos.

qa.a: What she actually wants this year, what she needs, and whether the option beats her own past, rather than how it looks next to someone else.

grounding: An adult weighs a transfer by her own needs and past rather than a colleague's highlight posts.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: Okay, Kavitha, you asked why I'm now the family's official 'do not let them order' person. I'm Wasim, and here's what happened. Saturday, at the cinema snack counter, the board had three options. Small popcorn, no drink, 250. Medium popcorn with a cold drink, 280. Large combo, 420. And my brain went: the medium is only thirty more than the small, and I get a drink free! Total bargain! I felt so smart ordering it. I don't even like cold drinks. It sat there going flat through the whole film. On the way home my cousin laughed and said nobody ever buys that small popcorn; it's only there to make the medium look cheap. I was annoyed, then kind of impressed. It worked on me completely, and I'd been so proud.

qa.a: The medium popcorn with a cold drink cost 280.

grounding: A teenager picks the mid-size combo because a poor third option makes it look like a bargain, and feels clever about it.

passage:
Friday. At the cinema in Leeds, Elizabeth studied the snack board. Small popcorn, £4. Small popcorn with a tiny drink, £6.20. Medium popcorn with a regular drink, £6.50. Large combo, £8.90. 'Only thirty pence more for loads more,' she told Irawati, and bought the medium. She felt very clever.

The next Friday. Back at the same counter, Irawati reached for the medium again. Elizabeth covered the small combo line with her hand. 'Do you even want a drink?' Irawati thought. 'Not really.' They each bought a small popcorn and shared a bottle of water from Elizabeth's bag.

qa.a: Irawati was probably surprised at first, then relieved to notice a drink was not really wanted.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: Ira, jaan, you want the biggest popcorn tub again? Sit. Let your Dilnaz Nani tell you about the day I was fifteen and very clever. Our town cinema had just started selling popcorn in paper cones. Small cone, two rupees. Medium cone, three rupees. And then a 'jumbo' for six rupees that was hardly bigger than the medium. My friend Shirin and I stood there, and I said, 'Look at the jumbo, what a cheat! The medium is the real bargain.' I bought the medium and felt so proud of myself all through the first half. Then at the interval my Abba saw me with half the cone still full. 'You never finish even a small one,' he said. I was cross with him. Only years later did I understand that the jumbo was there so girls like me would feel smart buying the medium.

qa.a: Dilnaz felt proud and clever at first, then cross when Abba pointed out the half-full cone.

qa.a: At the counter, before judging the jumbo; asking how much popcorn she would really eat would have pointed her to the small cone.

qa.q: How might Abba have seen the medium cone at the interval?
qa.a: To Abba it was simply too much popcorn for a girl who never finishes even a small one, not a bargain at all.

grounding: An elder recalls picking a mid-size popcorn because a poor third option made it look like a bargain.
